---
title: "5. Long-run risks: the endowment"
aliases:
  - /long-run-risks-model.html
---

[Chapter 4](04-epstein-zin-preferences.qmd) built an investor whose
marginal utility responds to news about future consumption. The
preferences add nothing if there is no such news. If consumption
growth is white noise, there is nothing persistent to learn about, and
the Epstein-Zin kernel prices almost exactly like the power-utility
kernel it replaced. The chapter supplies the other half, an endowment
in which expected growth genuinely moves.

The design comes from Bansal and Yaron (2004), and the idea fits in
one sentence. Consumption growth carries a small, highly persistent
component under transitory noise. The persistent component is tiny, a
few tenths of a percent per month, and it is nearly invisible in any
given year. A shock to it, however, is news about the next decade of
consumption rather than about the current year. The investor of
Chapter 4 prefers early resolution of uncertainty, so persistent news
is the kind she fears. Claims whose cash flows are levered to it must
pay a premium.

The same four equations also carry the entire cross section. Growth,
value, and market portfolios will differ in exactly one economically
meaningful way, which is how strongly their dividends load on the
persistent component. The loading, called cash-flow leverage, is the
model's characteristic and serves the purpose the CAPM assigns to
beta. It is a property of dividends, and it is measurable without
using any returns.

## Four equations

The endowment and the cash flows are (paper eq. 6):

$$
\Delta c_{t+1} = \mu_c + x_t + \sigma_t\, \eta_{t+1}
$$ {#eq-cons}

$$
x_{t+1} = \rho\, x_t + \varphi_x\, \sigma_t\, \epsilon_{t+1}
$$ {#eq-x}

$$
\sigma_{t+1}^2 = \bar\sigma^2 (1-\nu) + \nu\, \sigma_t^2 + \sigma_w\, w_{t+1}
$$ {#eq-vol}

$$
\Delta d_{i,t+1} = \mu_i + \phi_i\, x_t + \varphi_{\sigma,i}\, \sigma_t\, u_{i,t+1}
$$ {#eq-div}

with all shocks standard normal. In words, line by line:

- @eq-cons: the current month's consumption growth is a constant trend
  $\mu_c$, plus where expected growth currently stands ($x_t$), plus
  transitory noise. $x_t$ is the deviation of expected growth from its
  mean, and it is the time-varying counterpart of the constant $g$ a
  DCF plugs into its terminal value.
- @eq-x: expected growth itself drifts slowly. The persistence $\rho$
  is the model's most consequential parameter. The innovations are
  small ($\varphi_x$ scales them well below the transitory shock) but
  their effects last.
- @eq-vol: the volatility of everything is itself a slow-moving state.
  Economic uncertainty rises and recedes with persistence $\nu$ around
  the mean level $\bar\sigma^2$. The second state variable will price
  a distinct risk, but $x_t$ does the work in the current chapter.
- @eq-div: each claim $i$ pays dividends whose growth inherits expected
  consumption growth with **leverage** $\phi_i$, plus idiosyncratic
  noise scaled by $\varphi_{\sigma,i}$ (the residual $u_{i,t+1}$
  correlates with the consumption shock $\eta_{t+1}$ at a rate
  $\alpha_i$). $\phi_i$ is the only parameter in the whole model that
  differs across claims in an economically central way. Table II sets
  $\phi = 2.6$ for growth, $6.2$ for value, and $2.8$ for the
  market. A value firm's cash flows are levered to long-run news more
  than twice as strongly as a growth firm's. Everything the rest of the
  course says about the value premium follows from the one contrast.

## How long a shock to expected growth lasts

The persistence $\rho = 0.98$ is at a monthly frequency. Compute the
half-life of a shock to expected growth:

```{python}
import numpy as np
import lrrcs as lrr

cons = lrr.get_table_ii_params().cons
half_life = np.log(0.5) / np.log(cons.rho)
print(f"rho = {cons.rho} (monthly)  =>  "
      f"half-life of x_t = {half_life:.1f} months")
```

A piece of news about expected growth still has half its effect three
years later. The persistence is what separates @eq-x from noise. The
innovation to $x_t$ is on the order of $\varphi_x \sigma \approx$ two
hundredths of a percent per month, which is invisible next to the
transitory shock, but it compounds over a decade of expected
consumption. The investor of Chapter 4 prices news by its total future
weight rather than by its size in the current month.

## The persistence in the data

The i.i.d. benchmark is testable, because white-noise growth has zero
autocorrelation. Annual U.S. consumption growth does not:

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
# Data bootstrap: use the repo's committed CSVs, or fetch them when this
# notebook runs outside the repository.
from pathlib import Path
import urllib.request

DATA = Path("../../data")
if not DATA.exists():
    DATA = Path("data")
    DATA.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    base = ("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/tlorans/"
            "kiku-value-premium-replication/main/data/")
    for f in ("consumption_annual.csv",):
        if not (DATA / f).exists():
            urllib.request.urlretrieve(base + f, DATA / f)
```

```{python}
import pandas as pd

dc = pd.read_csv(DATA / "consumption_annual.csv")["dc"]
print(f"{len(dc)} years of annual consumption growth")
print(f"first autocorrelation (AC1): {dc.autocorr(1):.2f}")
```

An AC1 of 0.41 in 74 years of data is a clear rejection of white
noise. Growth in one year carries information about growth in the
next. The AC1 does not by itself prove the two-component structure of
@eq-cons and @eq-x. A persistent component of the calibrated size is
hard to detect, and the difficulty is the standing objection to the
whole approach, taken up in [Chapter 9](09-the-market-test.qmd). The
AC1 is, however, one of the moments the calibration below is fit to,
and the simulation at the end of the chapter reproduces it.

## The calibration in one table

Every number below is read from `lrr.get_table_ii_params()` at run
time, which is the same object every solver in the course consumes.
Units are monthly.

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
import pandas as pd
from great_tables import GT

KIKU_GT = dict(table_background_color="transparent", table_font_size="0.92rem",
               heading_title_font_size="1.05rem", heading_subtitle_font_size="0.85rem",
               source_notes_font_size="0.8rem", column_labels_font_weight="bold",
               data_row_padding="4px")

p = lrr.get_table_ii_params()
prefs, c = p.prefs, p.cons

calib_df = pd.DataFrame({
    "block": ["Preferences (household)"] * 4 + ["Consumption process (endowment)"] * 6,
    "parameter": ["delta", "gamma", "psi", "theta",
                  "mu", "rho", "phi_x", "sigma", "nu", "sigma_w"],
    "value": [f"{prefs.delta}", f"{prefs.gamma}", f"{prefs.psi}",
              f"{prefs.theta:.1f}",
              f"{c.mu}", f"{c.rho}", f"{c.phi_x}", f"{c.sigma}",
              f"{c.nu}", f"{c.sigma_w}"],
    "meaning": ["time preference", "risk aversion",
                "elasticity of intertemporal substitution",
                "derived, (1 - gamma) / (1 - 1/psi)",
                "mean monthly growth (about 1.8 %/yr)",
                "persistence of x_t (half-life about 3 yrs)",
                "sd of x_t shocks, relative to sigma",
                "mean monthly volatility (about 2.2 %/yr)",
                "persistence of volatility",
                "sd of volatility shocks"],
})
(
    GT(calib_df, rowname_col="parameter", groupname_col="block")
    .tab_header(title="Table II calibration, monthly units")
    .cols_label(value="value", meaning="meaning")
    .tab_source_note("Read from lrr.get_table_ii_params() at build time.")
    .tab_options(**KIKU_GT)
)
```

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
cash_df = pd.DataFrame(
    [{"claim": name, "mu": d.mu, "phi": d.phi,
      "phi_sigma": d.phi_sigma, "alpha": d.alpha}
     for name, d in p.dividends.items()]
)
(
    GT(cash_df)
    .tab_header(title="Table II cash-flow processes, monthly units")
    .cols_label(claim="claim", mu="mu_d", phi="phi",
                phi_sigma="phi_sigma", alpha="alpha")
    .fmt_number(columns=["mu"], decimals=4)
    .fmt_number(columns=["phi", "phi_sigma"], decimals=1)
    .fmt_number(columns=["alpha"], decimals=2)
    .tab_source_note("Read from lrr.get_table_ii_params() at build time.")
    .tab_options(**KIKU_GT)
)
```

Read the tables with the firewall in mind. The preference block and the
consumption block are disciplined by aggregate moments only: the mean,
volatility, and autocorrelation of consumption growth, and the
risk-free rate. The cash-flow block is disciplined by dividends only.
[Chapter 8](08-calibrating-cash-flows.qmd) estimates the leverages
$\phi_i$ by regressing dividend growth on a moving average of
consumption growth, with no returns anywhere in the procedure. Returns
appear once, at the very end of the course, as the thing to be
explained.

## What a path looks like

Numbers on a page understate how well hidden $x_t$ is. Simulate forty
years of the economy and plot monthly consumption growth against the
expected-growth state underneath it:

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| fig-cap: "Forty years of simulated monthly consumption growth (gray) and the expected-growth component μ_c + x_t underneath it (dark red). The persistent state is an order of magnitude smaller than the noise, yet it carries the priced risk."
from plotnine import (ggplot, aes, geom_line, geom_hline, labs,
                      scale_color_manual, theme_minimal, theme,
                      element_blank, element_line, element_text)

sim = lrr.Dynamics(lrr.get_table_ii_params(), seed=3).simulate_cashflows(480)
path_df = pd.DataFrame({
    "years": np.arange(480) / 12,
    "realized": 100 * sim["dc"],
    "expected": 100 * (cons.mu + sim["x"]),
})

plot = (
    ggplot(path_df, aes("years"))
    + geom_line(aes(y="realized", color='"realized growth Δc"'), size=0.5)
    + geom_line(aes(y="expected", color='"expected growth μ + x"'), size=0.9)
    + geom_hline(yintercept=100 * cons.mu, color="#1b1714",
                 linetype="dotted", size=0.4)
    + scale_color_manual(values={"realized growth Δc": "#b0aca6",
                                 "expected growth μ + x": "#7a1f1f"})
    + labs(x="years", y="monthly growth (%)")
    + theme_minimal(base_size=11)
    + theme(figure_size=(6.5, 3.4), text=element_text(color="#2d2926"),
            panel_grid_minor=element_blank(),
            panel_grid_major=element_line(color="#e2d6c4", size=0.4),
            axis_line=element_line(color="#1b1714", size=0.5),
            legend_title=element_blank(), legend_position="top")
)
plot.show()
```

The gray series is what an econometrician observes, and the dark line
is the state the investor is afraid of. Distinguishing the second
inside the first from a few decades of data is hard, and the
paper does not claim otherwise. The model claims that prices respond
to the dark line, which is why valuations will turn out to be
informative about $x_t$ in a way realized consumption is not.

## Simulation to annual data: a warning about aggregation

One detail affects every comparison of the model's monthly output to
annual data, and skipping it corrupts the comparison. The paper
builds annual consumption the way NIPA builds it. First, sum twelve
monthly levels to an annual level. Then take log growth of the annual
sums. The level construction is not the same as summing twelve monthly
log growth rates, and the difference is visible in exactly the moment
the chapter uses:

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
dyn = lrr.Dynamics(lrr.get_table_ii_params(), seed=0)
dc_m = dyn.simulate_cashflows(12 * 20000)["dc"]

# NIPA convention: annual level = sum of 12 monthly levels, then log growth
level = np.exp(np.cumsum(dc_m))
annual_level = level.reshape(-1, 12).sum(axis=1)
g_levels = np.diff(np.log(annual_level))

# Naive alternative: sum the 12 monthly log growth rates
g_logs = dc_m.reshape(-1, 12).sum(axis=1)[1:]

def ac1(y):
    return np.corrcoef(y[:-1], y[1:])[0, 1]

print(f"model annual consumption growth, 20,000 simulated years")
print(f"  AC1, aggregating levels (NIPA convention): {ac1(g_levels):.2f}")
print(f"  AC1, summing log growth rates:             {ac1(g_logs):.2f}")
```

::: {.callout-warning title="Time-aggregate levels, not log growth"}
The same simulated economy prints an annual AC1 of 0.43 when monthly
levels are summed within the year, and only 0.20 when monthly log
growth rates are summed. The 0.43 matches the model AC1 in the paper's
Table III and sits next to the 0.41 measured in the data above.
Summing levels within the year overlaps adjacent years' information
and adds persistence that the log-growth aggregation throws away. A
simulation that sums log growth will understate the paper's annual
autocorrelation every time. It is the single most common way to fail
to reproduce Table III.
:::

## Takeaways

- The endowment is four equations: persistent expected growth $x_t$
  inside consumption growth, slowly moving uncertainty
  $\sigma_t^2$, and dividends levered to $x_t$ claim by claim.
- $x_t$ is small but long lasting. With $\rho = 0.98$ monthly, a shock
  keeps half its effect after 34 months, and long-run news is what the
  Chapter 4 investor prices.
- The data reject white-noise consumption growth. Annual AC1 is 0.41 in
  74 years, and the calibrated model reproduces it (0.43) under the
  correct level aggregation.
- The cross section enters through one parameter, the cash-flow
  leverage $\phi_i$ (growth 2.6, market 2.8, value 6.2). It is a
  property of dividends, estimated in
  [Chapter 8](08-calibrating-cash-flows.qmd) without returns.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Recall"}

Answer from memory before opening.

1. Name the four equations of the endowment in words.
2. How long does a shock to expected growth keep half its effect at
   $\rho = 0.98$ monthly?
3. Across the three claims, exactly one parameter differs in an
   economically central way. Which, and what does it measure?

**Answers.**

1. Consumption growth carries a persistent expected-growth component
   plus noise; expected growth drifts with persistence $\rho$; volatility
   itself moves slowly; and each claim's dividend growth loads on the
   persistent component with leverage $\phi_i$.
2. About 34 months, three years.
3. The cash-flow leverage $\phi_i$: how strongly the claim's dividend
   growth moves with the persistent component of consumption (2.6
   growth, 2.8 market, 6.2 value).

:::

## Exercises

1. Recompute the half-life of $x_t$ for $\rho = 0.95$ and
   $\rho = 0.90$. Then look ahead to the elasticity
   $A_1 = (\phi - 1/\psi)/(1 - \kappa_1 \rho)$ of
   [Chapter 6](06-log-linear-solution.qmd) and say, before computing
   anything, which claim's valuation loses more when persistence falls.
2. Rerun the aggregation cell with `phi_x = 0` (rebuild the parameters
   with `lrr.ConsumptionParams(phi_x=0.0)` inside a `ModelParams`).
   With no persistent component at all, what AC1 does each aggregation
   convention print, and what does the gap between them tell you about
   the level convention on its own?
3. Simulate two economies with `lrr.Dynamics(..., seed=7)`, identical
   except $\rho = 0.98$ versus $\rho = 0.90$, and plot
   $\mu_c + x_t$ for both. How does the figure change, and at which
   frequency would you now look for the state in the data?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Check your answer"}

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
import copy

# Exercise 1: half-lives at lower persistence
for rho in (0.95, 0.90):
    print(f"rho = {rho}:  half-life = "
          f"{np.log(0.5) / np.log(rho):.1f} months")

# Exercise 2: no persistent component at all
p0 = copy.deepcopy(lrr.get_table_ii_params())
p0.cons.phi_x = 0.0
dc0 = lrr.Dynamics(p0, seed=0).simulate_cashflows(12 * 20000)["dc"]
level0 = np.exp(np.cumsum(dc0))
ann0 = level0.reshape(-1, 12).sum(axis=1)
g_lvl = np.diff(np.log(ann0))
g_log = dc0.reshape(-1, 12).sum(axis=1)[1:]
print(f"AC1, level convention:  {np.corrcoef(g_lvl[:-1], g_lvl[1:])[0,1]:.2f}")
print(f"AC1, log convention:    {np.corrcoef(g_log[:-1], g_log[1:])[0,1]:.2f}")
```

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| fig-cap: "The expected-growth state at rho = 0.98 (dark red) against rho = 0.90 (gray). At the lower persistence the state decays much faster."
from plotnine import ggplot, aes, geom_line, labs, scale_color_manual, \
    theme_minimal, theme, element_blank, element_line, element_text

T = 480
x98 = lrr.Dynamics(lrr.get_table_ii_params(), seed=7).simulate_cashflows(T)["x"]
p90 = copy.deepcopy(lrr.get_table_ii_params())
p90.cons.rho = 0.90
x90 = lrr.Dynamics(p90, seed=7).simulate_cashflows(T)["x"]
paths = pd.DataFrame({
    "years": np.arange(T) / 12,
    "rho = 0.98": 100 * (cons.mu + x98),
    "rho = 0.90": 100 * (cons.mu + x90),
}).melt(id_vars="years", var_name="rho", value_name="expected")

(
    ggplot(paths, aes("years", "expected", color="rho"))
    + geom_line(size=0.8)
    + scale_color_manual(values={"rho = 0.98": "#7a1f1f",
                                 "rho = 0.90": "#b0aca6"})
    + labs(x="years", y="expected growth (%)")
    + theme_minimal(base_size=11)
    + theme(figure_size=(6.5, 2.8), text=element_text(color="#2d2926"),
            panel_grid_minor=element_blank(),
            panel_grid_major=element_line(color="#e2d6c4", size=0.4),
            axis_line=element_line(color="#1b1714", size=0.5),
            legend_title=element_blank(), legend_position="top")
)
```

The half-life falls from 34 months to about 14 at rho = 0.95 and about 7 at
rho = 0.90, and the claim that loses most is value, whose phi puts most
of its valuation on the persistent state. With phi_x = 0 the log
convention prints a near-zero AC1 but the level convention still prints
0.24, so the overlap in the level construction adds persistence on its
own. Reaching the 0.43 the paper reports needs the persistent component
on top of the convention.
The figure shows the state decaying quickly at rho = 0.90, so you would
look for it in shorter moving averages.
